children.title: Court Sets Aside HUD's 2025 Continuum of Care Funding Notices
children.description_short: A federal court ruled that HUD's November and December 2025 Continuum of Care notices violated the Administrative Procedure Act and set them aside.
children.description_medium: On June 29, 2026, a federal court set aside HUD’s November and December 2025 Continuum of Care funding notices. California’s attorney general said the ruling found the notices unlawful under the Administrative Procedure Act and preserved billions in homelessness funding. This decision concerned FY2025 notices; the separate August 2026 ruling addressed a later FY2026 notice.
children.description_long: A federal court ruled on June 29, 2026 that HUD’s November and December 2025 Continuum of Care funding notices could not stand. California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office said the court found that HUD had made material changes to the program without following the Administrative Procedure Act. The ruling set aside the notices and preserved approximately $3.6 billion in funding for homelessness programs while litigation proceeded. The Continuum of Care program funds local and regional systems that coordinate housing and services for people experiencing homelessness. The June decision concerned the prior fiscal year’s competition and its funding notices. It should be described as a court ruling about those particular notices, rather than a blanket reversal of all HUD policy changes or a finding on every asserted consequence for people in permanent supportive housing. A later, separate August 2026 decision addressed HUD’s FY2026 notice and should retain its own date and procedural posture.

children.title: Court Sets Aside HUD's FY2026 Continuum of Care Notice
children.description_short: A federal court set aside HUD’s FY2026 Continuum of Care notice on August 7, 2026.
children.description_medium: On August 7, 2026, a federal court blocked HUD’s FY2026 Continuum of Care notice changes. California’s attorney general reported that the court found the policy revisions unlawful and preserved permanent supportive housing funding. HUD’s program page confirms the program’s annual competition context; the court ruling remains a separate action from the June decision about FY2025 notices.
children.description_long: On August 7, 2026, a federal court blocked changes HUD had made to the FY2026 Continuum of Care funding competition. California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office said the court found the administration’s revisions unlawful and prevented the new notice from diverting funds away from permanent supportive housing. HUD describes Continuum of Care as a competitive program that supports community systems serving people experiencing homelessness. The August ruling concerned the FY2026 notice and followed a June ruling that set aside HUD’s earlier FY2025 notices. These are separate court orders involving different annual funding competitions; they should not be collapsed into one ruling or described as three separate wins without identifying the orders. The state release characterizes the result as protecting permanent supportive housing, while the HUD competition page supplies the administrative program context. The available sources do not establish the held claim that exactly 97,000 people would be pushed onto the street.

proposal.split_guard: Separate FY2025 court ruling (June 29) from FY2026 court ruling (August 7). Do not reuse the three-block sequence or merge the fiscal-year notices.

excluded_original_claims: Three blocks of the same changes in March, June and August; $3.0B-to-$2.4B sequence; exactly 97,000 people pushed onto the street.

children.description_long: On June 9, 2026, the Bureau of Land Management held a quarterly oil-and-gas lease sale in Wyoming. BLM reported that 102 parcels covering approximately 114,439 acres were leased, generating total receipts of $34,706,638. The agency said combined lease bonus bids and rentals are distributed between the federal government and the state where parcels are located. This is a completed sale and its reported acreage and proceeds can be stated directly with attribution to BLM. The release does not establish the original card’s assertions about the sale being near Yellowstone, overlap with state-designated mule-deer or pronghorn migration corridors, or the terms of a separate proposed auction. Those claims concern distinct land parcels or future offerings and require separate maps, sale notices, or environmental records. The June sale should therefore be described as its own event, with location, number of parcels, acreage and proceeds drawn from the BLM announcement rather than generalized to all 2026 Wyoming leasing.

proposal.split_guard: The February 3, 2025 Interior orders and June 9, 2026 Wyoming lease sale are distinct. Do not combine them or attach the unverified 250,000-acre, corridor-overlap, 28-day deadline or leasing-mandate claims.

children.title: Trump orders U.S. withdrawal process from the World Health Organization
children.description_short: Trump orders U.S. withdrawal process from the World Health Organization.
children.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order directing the United States to begin withdrawing from the World Health Organization. It directed officials to pause future U.S. funding, recall or reassign U.S. personnel and contractors, and suspend negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement while withdrawal proceeded. The order began a withdrawal process; it did not immediately end U.S. membership.
children.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order directing the United States to begin withdrawing from the World Health Organization. The order instructed the Secretary of State and the Director of the Office of Management and Budget to pause future transfers of U.S. government funds to WHO, recall and reassign U.S. personnel and contractors working with the organization, and suspend negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement. It also directed officials to identify alternative partners for relevant public-health activities. The order initiated a withdrawal process under the organization’s notice requirements; it did not immediately remove the United States from WHO on the day it was signed. The later decision to withdraw from UNESCO was made in a separate July 2025 announcement and under a different international organization’s procedures. The original combined title therefore conflates two actions separated by six months and involving distinct institutions.

proposal.split_guard: WHO withdrawal-process order (January 20) and UNESCO withdrawal announcement (July 22) are separate organizations, dates and instruments. Do not state immediate departure from either organization.

excluded_original_claims: Both withdrawals occurred January 20, 2025; immediate withdrawal from either organization.

record.title: Trump threatens to revoke Harvard’s tax-exempt status
record.description_short: Trump said his administration would revoke Harvard’s tax-exempt status; Harvard called the threat unlawful and unprecedented.
record.description_medium: On May 2, 2025, Trump posted that his administration would take away Harvard’s tax-exempt status. Reuters described it as a renewed threat after a similar April 15 post. Harvard called revocation unlawful and unprecedented. The university was already challenging a federal freeze of about $2.2 billion in grants, most of which supported medical and scientific research. Reuters also described government demands on governance and viewpoints; no revocation was reported.
record.description_long: On May 2, 2025, President Donald Trump posted that his administration would take away Harvard University’s tax-exempt status. Reuters reported that Trump gave no explanation in that post and described it as a renewed threat following a similar statement on April 15. Harvard responded that revocation would be unlawful and unprecedented, and said there was no legal basis to rescind its status. At the time, Harvard was already suing over a federal freeze of about $2.2 billion in grants, most of which supported medical and scientific research. Reuters also reported that the university had faced demands concerning governance, faculty and student viewpoints, masks, and diversity initiatives after rejecting the administration’s terms. The article distinguishes Trump’s threat from an actual IRS revocation: IRS representatives did not respond to Reuters’ questions, and the White House said any IRS action would be independent. The record should therefore describe a public threat directed at Harvard on May 2, not a completed tax-status change or a February action against multiple universities.

excluded_original_claims: February 2025 date; threats to multiple universities; completed revocation; asserted DEI motive.

record.title: Trump Revokes Federal Contractor Affirmative-Action Order
record.description_short: On January 21, 2025, Trump revoked Executive Order 11246 and directed changes to federal contractor affirmative-action requirements, with a 90-day transition period.
record.description_medium: On January 21, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14173, which revoked Executive Order 11246 and directed the Labor Department’s contractor-compliance office to cease promoting diversity and holding contractors responsible for affirmative action. The order allowed contractors to continue following the prior regulatory scheme for 90 days. It was signed January 21, not January 20.
record.description_long: On January 21, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14173, “Ending Illegal Discrimination and Restoring Merit-Based Opportunity.” The order revoked Executive Order 11246, which had governed equal employment opportunity requirements for federal contractors. It directed the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs to cease promoting diversity and holding federal contractors and subcontractors responsible for affirmative action. The order also required federal contracts and grants to include terms concerning compliance with federal anti-discrimination laws and certifications about unlawful DEI programs. For 90 days, contractors could continue complying with the regulatory scheme that had been in effect on January 20. The title should therefore identify the January 21 order and its contractor provisions rather than claim that every contracting requirement ended on January 20. The White House text is primary evidence of the order’s date and terms; broader implementation effects are outside this event description.

excluded_original_claims: All DEI federal contracting requirements ended; original January 20 date.
